profile.reading: This OpenStreetMap record in Johnson County, Iowa, near Coralville, is tagged as a data center under the name ForceAmp.com. Reverse geocoding the stored coordinates finds the address is now occupied by a RE/MAX real estate office rather than any technology business, indicating whatever tenant the ForceAmp name once described has since moved out or closed. Separately, the ForceAmp name itself points to Salesforce integration software rather than a data center: the domains forceamp.com and dbamp.com both currently redirect to CData Software's dbAmp product, a tool that connects Microsoft SQL Server to Salesforce data, and dbAmp's own marketing material lists forceamp among its search keywords, indicating a historical connection between the ForceAmp name and this small business software product rather than any audio equipment brand or IT hosting company. Taken together, the evidence points to a small software company office, most likely one that built or sold Salesforce integration tools under or alongside the ForceAmp name, later absorbed into CData Software, rather than a facility that ever functioned as a commercial data center housing servers for outside tenants. No capacity, tenant or infrastructure figures are offered because none could be confirmed, and the address today appears to house an unrelated real estate business.

reading.body:
ForceAmp.com is not a data center and should not be counted toward Iowa AI infrastructure capacity.

The record is an OpenStreetMap entry in Johnson County, Iowa tagged as a data center under the ForceAmp.com name. A reverse geocode of the stored coordinates returns a RE/MAX real estate office at that address today. The ForceAmp name traces to a Salesforce integration tool, dbAmp, now part of CData Software, not to an infrastructure operator. The evidence points to a small software office that has since closed or moved, not a facility that housed servers for outside tenants.

This matters because facility counts are an input to estimates of regional compute supply. A miscount inflates the denominator without adding a single megawatt. Iowa has 52 mapped data center facilities, and only 2 of them publish power consumption figures, totaling 18 MW. This location contributes nothing to that sum. The gap between 52 mapped facilities and 2 with published figures is the more useful signal: most of what gets counted as data center capacity in the state is unverified.

The data does not say what the site was before the real estate office, when any software business there operated, or whether a building of any size ever stood at these coordinates. It also does not establish that other OpenStreetMap data center tags in Iowa are wrong. It establishes that this one is, and that the tag alone is not evidence of compute.
